builder_plan.scenario: A self-hosted assistant is too expensive because its model uses most of the GPU memory.
builder_plan.change: Try the paper's supported lower-precision weights on a copy of your serving setup.
builder_plan.baseline: The same model at its original precision, on the same GPU.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Peak memory, task pass rate, latency, and total serving cost at the same context and load.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: End-to-End MXFP8 Reinforcement Learning on Blackwell: What Matching Buys, When It Pays Off, and How It Fails
summary: The method replaces BF16 compute in RL post-training with MXFP8 on both the Megatron/Transformer Engine learner and the vLLM/SGLang sampler, provided both share the same quantization grid and weight synchronization preserves seven stated correctness conditions. It requires Blackwell-generation (B200) GPUs, verl infrastructure, and sequence lengths long enough to amortize a fixed per-micro-batch quantization cost that is otherwise host-bound overhead. It can fail through train-rollout KL divergence when sampler and learner grids mismatch (2x KL on MoE from the first step), through silently broken weight synchronization (five of seven observed failures were silent), and through net slowdowns on short-sequence dense workloads; without a quantized KV cache, BF16 remains 2.5-10x more consistent.
rationale: The technique depends on B200-class hardware and a multi-engine RL stack that the reader's 24 GB GPU and limited budget cannot provision, so it is relevant only as guidance for future infrastructure decisions.
technique: End-to-end MXFP8 RL with matched sampler-learner quantization grid

claims.statement: The method replaces BF16 compute in RL post-training with MXFP8 on both the Megatron/Transformer Engine learner and the vLLM/SGLang sampler, provided both share the same quantization grid and weight synchronization preserves seven stated correctness conditions. It requires Blackwell-generation (B200) GPUs, verl infrastructure, and sequence lengths long enough to amortize a fixed per-micro-batch quantization cost that is otherwise host-bound overhead. It can fail through train-rollout KL divergence when sampler and learner grids mismatch (2x KL on MoE from the first step), through silently broken weight synchronization (five of seven observed failures were silent), and through net slowdowns on short-sequence dense workloads; without a quantized KV cache, BF16 remains 2.5-10x more consistent.
MXFP8 cuts MoE step time by 10.7% and generation time by 24% end to end, but slows a short-sequence dense workload by 5% and pays off in dense training only above roughly 4.5k tokens per micro-batch.
